# CMake

Cross-platform build-system generator: a `CMakeLists.txt` describes targets, and CMake emits Makefiles,
Ninja files or an MSVC solution for whatever toolchain is present. The usual reason to reach for it in
a C++ project is portability — one description, many generators.

It appears once in [[optimization-methods]], for `first_project`'s
{{permutation-flow-shop-scheduling}} benchmark, and is **not carried forward**.

## The broken first line — a §10 contradiction, both claims recorded

| # | Claim | Source | `valid_from` | `valid_to` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `first_project/CMakeLists.txt` **cannot configure**: `cmake_minimum_required` is missing its `VERSION` keyword | `first_project/CMakeLists.txt` | 2026-03-28 | 2026-08-01 |
| 2 | It configures: the keyword is present and `project()` declares `CXX` | `git show d116a84`, read 2026-08-05 | 2026-08-01 | null |

For the entire life of the coursework, `first_project/CMakeLists.txt` opened with:

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(3.16)
project(PFSP)
```

**The `VERSION` keyword is missing.** The command's signature is
`cmake_minimum_required(VERSION <min>)`, so `cmake_minimum_required(3.16)` is a hard configure error,
not a warning. The rest of the file is fine — C++17 required, `include_directories(include)`, a single
`pfsp` executable over the 12 sources — but nothing downstream ever ran, because configuration aborted
on line 1.

It now reads `cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)` / `project(PFSP CXX)`, repaired on 2026-08-01:

> Optimization Methods, git commit d116a84 "Fix the CMake invocation that stopped the build
> configuring", 2026-08-01

The naming of the language in `project()` is the second half of the same repair and easy to miss.
`project(PFSP)` enables `C` and `CXX` by default, so CMake probes for a C compiler this project
never uses — a second failure waiting behind the first. The commit says so in its own words, and
says it triaged before repairing: *"all twelve sources compile clean under `g++ -std=c++17`, so the
C++ was never the problem. Verified by an out-of-source configure and build that links `pfsp.exe`."*
Fixing only the visible error would have moved the failure rather than removed it.

What follows is the analysis of why the defect survived so long. The repair does not touch it: it
is dated 2026-08-01, three weeks after the course ended, and its own message records that the
project still has no unit tests. Nobody hit this by following the README, which is the point.

The README nonetheless presented CMake as the **recommended** build path. So for the whole course the
documented happy path did not work as written, which lines up with the other evidence: a prebuilt
**`pfsp.exe` is committed** and kept current (`287876f build: update compiled pfsp executable`),
tracked despite the root `.gitignore` carrying an `*.exe` rule. The executable was the actual run
path; CMake was aspirational.

`confidence: high` — both versions of the file read directly. The repaired configure step is **not**
independently re-run here: CMake is not installed on the auditing machine, so the only evidence that
it now configures is the commit's own statement that it was verified out-of-source. That is weaker
evidence than reading the file, and is worth less than it looks — see the residual gap below.

This is a distinct species of [[documentation-drift]]: not documentation that fell behind working
code, but documentation for code that never worked. Ordinary drift is caught by anyone following the
README; this was not, which is the tell that nobody followed it — including the author, who had a
working binary.

**The repair did not reach the README.** `first_project/README.md` still says *"From repository root:
`cmake -S . -B build`"*, and there is no `CMakeLists.txt` at the git repository root — it is in
`first_project/`. Read as written, against the root the sentence names, the command still fails; read
as "the project root", it now works. One line of the documented path is fixed and the line above it is
still ambiguous. `confidence: high` on the file layout, `low` on which root the sentence means.

## Dropped for the second project

`final_project/mdvrp` does not use CMake at all. It has a hand-written `Makefile`
(`-std=c++17 -O2 -static -Wall -Wextra`) plus raw `g++` invocations recorded in `docs/commands.txt`,
building six executables from one header-only include tree. For a standard-library-only,
header-only-dependency project targeting one toolchain (MinGW), a 20-line Makefile does genuinely
carry less ceremony than CMake — but the switch is undocumented.

- **TODO:** no recorded reason for dropping CMake between the two projects. Whether the broken
  `cmake_minimum_required` line was ever hit and prompted the switch, or the Makefile was simply
  preferred, is unrecoverable from the repo. `confidence: low` on the causal link.
- **TODO:** the "recommended" CMake instructions in `first_project/README.md` still name the
  repository root, which holds no `CMakeLists.txt`. The build file was repaired on 2026-08-01 and the
  sentence pointing at it was not, so the documentation is now one step behind the code rather than
  ahead of it — ordinary [[documentation-drift]], where it used to be the rarer kind.

## Build verification across the repo

There is **no CI anywhere** — no `.github/`, no build check. The claim that all seven C++ sources
compile clean under `-std=c++17 -O2 -Wall` is attested by hand in `docs/DATA_VERIFICATION.md`, dated
2026-07-09, by the author. That is the same auditing-instead-of-testing posture as the rest of the
repo — see [[generated-audit-artifact]] and the absence of any unit tests noted on
[[optimization-methods]].
